A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same ParaHome system and dataset. Their complete text, equations, tables, figures, and appendices are readable, allowing retained, relocated, added, and removed material to be matched reliably.

before.justification: v1 reports original capture-system experiments, including marker tracking, reprojection errors, hand alignment, tracking recovery, and dataset contact statistics.

after.justification: v2 retains capture-system experiments and adds original motion-generation results, ablations, and pose-reconstruction evaluations on synthesized images.

M1.justification: v2 adds implemented generative procedures beyond v1's prospective task formulations: MDM-based text-conditioned motion generation with latent interpolation, an object-conditioned transformer, and ControlNet-based RGB synthesis. It also introduces learned SMPL-X fitting using an autoencoder and latent optimization (Sections 3.5 and 5; Appendix C.5).

E1.justification: v1 evaluates capture accuracy and home-interaction data. v2 additionally uses HumanML3D for motion-generation training and AMASS for body-model fitting, and evaluates text-conditioned motion, object-guided motion, and hand/object reconstruction from synthetic images. These substantially expand actual training and task coverage beyond the retained room and 22 objects.

E2.justification: The original capture-system comparators remain. v2 adds comparisons of single-dataset versus mixed-data motion models and models with versus without relative spatial cues (Tables 2-3). Tables 7-8 add IST-Net/GenPose++ and Pose2Mesh/HaMeR comparison rows; IST-Net and Pose2Mesh appear only on reference datasets, not ParaHome.

E3.justification: v2 introduces balanced HumanML3D/ParaHome training, evaluation on a mixed test set, 30/60/90-frame motion windows, and new generation/reconstruction metrics. Collection increases from 30 participants and 440 minutes to 38 and 486. The virtual-marker criterion is also rephrased from four markers tracked throughout a window to four tracked in every frame; whether its implementation changed is unstated.

E4.justification: New analyses test training-data mixture, relative spatial conditioning, body representation, temporal window length, and text conditioning for image synthesis (Tables 2-3 and 9; Figure 13). Figures 14-15 add occlusion failure cases. Original capture robustness tests remain, while v1's per-object contact-frequency analysis is removed.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run summaries, confidence intervals, or significance tests. v2's additional tables retain point-estimate reporting; diffusion noise definitions do not constitute experimental uncertainty reporting.

E6.justification: Original measurements, including reprojection errors of 1.021/1.016 pixels and 11 mm hand-alignment error, remain unchanged. New Tables 2-3 and 7-9 report generation and reconstruction outcomes, including mixed-training FID 0.85 and lower position errors but greater foot skating with spatial conditioning. These are new experiments, not v1-to-v2 performance gains. v1's contact-ratio table is removed.

T1.justification: Formal content expands from generic HOI mappings and capture-calibration objectives to conditional diffusion distributions, denoising losses, latent interpolation, object-conditioned motion mappings, and SMPL-X latent-fitting optimization. Existing articulation derivations largely remain. The substantial addition concerns mathematical formulations; no theorem or proof is added.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains a room-scale system and dataset combining body, finger, and articulated-object motion. v2 replaces the stated contribution of introducing future research tasks with presenting two example generative applications, and softens v1's categorical uniqueness language. The core research objective remains stable.

C2.justification: v2 adds interpretations about blending locomotion and manipulation, coordinate-representation tradeoffs, and reconstruction failures attributed to occlusion and articulation. Synthetic RGB generation substantially extends the applicability discussion beyond v1's warning about biased captured images. Appendix B.1 also explicitly acknowledges that markers can influence natural human motion.

D1.justification: v2 adds FABRIK/autoencoder fitting details, image-generation inputs, and object-motion training settings, including AdamW, learning rate 0.0001, 1500 epochs, and batch size 32. Data availability changes from promised to reported public availability. Conversely, the full action list, scenario-construction details, and detailed contact-computation documentation from v1 are removed.

R1.justification: Related work expands substantially into hybrid capture and recent motion/interaction synthesis, including MDM, DiffH2O, Text2HOI, and InterTrack. The dataset comparison replaces several older hand-focused datasets with Chairs, NeuralDome, OAKINK2, TACO, and TRUMANS. v1's first-dataset and frame-count superiority positioning is also softened.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, and related work are extensively rewritten. Capture and acquisition material is consolidated into Section 3, validation precedes the expanded generative-modeling section, and dataset documentation is reorganized in the appendix. These are substantial narrative and structural changes beyond the added experiments.

P2.justification: v2 merges setup/marker, object/articulation, and body/hand-calibration figures, and rearranges the retained system plots. It adds fitting, generation, architecture, and failure-case displays. The dataset comparison changes from frame counts to hours and revises its rows; original action/contact tables and extensive contact visualizations are removed.

improvement.justification: v1's generative-modeling motivation is largely prospective. v2 supplies implemented tasks, quantitative evaluations, and targeted ablations (Section 5; Tables 2-3 and 9), substantially strengthening evidence for downstream utility. Added fitting and synthetic-image evaluations further support usability. Removed scenario/contact documentation and the inconsistent 207 versus 208 capture counts weaken reproducibility, but do not outweigh the substantial evidentiary gains.
